approachQuestion.prompt:
Inspection posts

Each sensor is active over a closed integer interval [left,right]. Placing an inspection post at any integer coordinate checks all sensors whose intervals contain that coordinate. Return the minimum number of posts needed to check every sensor; endpoints count as contained.

Example 1: intervals=[[1,4],[3,7],[6,9]] → 2, for posts at 4 and 9.
Example 2: intervals=[[1,2],[2,3]] → 1.
Example 3: intervals=[] → 0.

Constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 100000; 0 ≤ left ≤ right ≤ 10^9; intervals are unsorted. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Copy intervals and sort by increasing right endpoint. Scan in that order, placing a new post at the current right endpoint whenever there is no previous post or the interval starts strictly after the last post.
options.feedback: The earliest-ending uncovered interval needs a post at or before its right endpoint. Moving such a post to that endpoint cannot lose any still-uncovered interval that it checked: their right endpoints are no smaller. Repeat after skipping intervals hit by that post.

options.text: Place a post at the left endpoint of the earliest-ending uncovered interval.
options.feedback: This can miss overlaps to its right. For [[1,4],[3,5]], this puts posts at 1 and 3, although a single post at 4 checks both.

options.text: Group intervals by transitive overlap and use one post per group.
options.feedback: A chain of overlaps need not share one coordinate. For [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4]], all lie in one overlap group, but no point hits the first and last; two posts are required.

options.text: Enumerate every legal sequence of decisions, evaluate each complete candidate, and return the best result.
options.feedback: Exhaustive search can find the right result, but revisits combinations of decisions that the safe local rule resolves directly. The number of candidates grows far beyond what the input limit permits.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method, regardless of your previous choice. The fixed frontier method copies the records, uses stable top-down comparison merge sort with one reusable linear merge buffer, and then makes the scan described above. Count copying, the buffer, and the recursion stack. Let n be the number of input records or positions. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

options.text: Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n)
Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(1)

feedback.reason: Sort interval ends and make one constant-state covering scan.

messages.text: The input copy and merge buffer require linear auxiliary storage.
The scan does not compare every pair; merge sort sets the time bound.
The unsorted input must also be ordered by the specified comparison sort.

details: Sorting takes O(n log n) worst-case time; the copy and scan are linear. The copy and reusable buffer take O(n) space, dominating the O(log n) recursive sort stack.
